en: Once, having arrived alone in the city of Ṛtuparṇa, the King of Niṣadha, the destroyer of Kali, spoke these words to the king: (1)
"Having indeed abandoned my own country, O King, I have come here as one named Bāhuka;
in the driving of horses, there is no one on earth equal to me. (2)
I am indeed to be seen with skill by one who knows the meaning;
I also know the preparation of food, as well as that of meat. (3)
Eatable, chewable, lickable, suckable, and drinkable, along with milk products—these are the varieties of the six tastes, distinguished by their pure and prepared forms. (4)
And for all condiments, the seasoning with salt and other ingredients—without these, and even with water, there is a variegated cooking that brings forth flavor. (5)
Whatever crafts exist in this world, and whatever else is difficult to obtain—
even that which has been rendered flavorful by me— is more difficult to find than the nectar of immortality.
By consuming it with effort, one’s health shall certainly be secured;
it always destroys diseases born of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman) through a single application, just as Tryambaka [Śiva] destroyed Tripura. ||7||
Fever arising from the disorder of indigestion, such as that caused by Maheśvara and others;
heart disease, consumption (rājayakṣmā) and other ailments, as well as colic and the like;
fistula-in-ano, diarrhea, and likewise disorders of the three humors combined (saṃnipāta).
In this manner, he destroys the entire web of diseases, beginning with these. ||9||
"I shall strive to do all that; O Ṛtuparṇa, support me.
Having said this, she took up residence in the palace of Ṛtuparṇa. Once, that king, the best of monarchs, summoned her.
"From where were these arts obtained? Tell us something pleasing, my dear. (11)
Having heard those words, he spoke virtuously;
"Listen, O Indra among kings, to the true origin of my knowledge. (12)
The lords of the gods have arrived for the sake of the self-choice marriage of the princess of Vidarbha;
I too have come there, and I was seen by them on the road.
There the gods spoke these words to me for the sake of deception:
"O tiger among men, act in such a way that the daughter of Bhīma will choose you.
When they had said, "Do so indeed," they further said, "May it be well with you."
Having assumed the form of messengers, they truly sought me out;
and upon beholding the King of Niṣadha, they bestowed unsurpassed boons.
First, Indra himself, being pleased, granted the power of invisibility.
Then he bestowed upon him the power of consuming oblations without fuel;
then the mastery over the essence of food, and the son of the Sun (Yama) granted worldly success;
and Varuṇa gave the mastery over water, O best of beings, all without effort.
"Thus, O gods, those sciences, having granted him their own station, departed.
Having heard these words of his, the king, filled with wonder, said to him:
"This science is indeed supernatural; residing in you, it is difficult for men to attain."
"Therefore, for the sake of our welfare, please show her to us in truth by way of illustration; for we have a great curiosity regarding her vision.
When the lord of kings had spoken thus, the prince of Niṣadha replied once more:
In this matter, I have composed this work for the benefit of the world,
titled *Pākadarpaṇa*, through the grace of Lokapāla.
By its very examination, various culinary preparations are seen.
O Lord, I shall now describe the characteristics of a cook in brief:
one born in his own country, wise, endowed with all auspicious marks, possessed of virtuous conduct, and born of a distinguished family. (22–23)
Peaceful, self-controlled, and generous in nature, he was honored by kings and possessed a pure smile.
Devoted to his own wife, he was pure and avoided the wives of others. (24) He was moderate in speech, always a giver, compassionate, and eloquent.
The wise one, knowing the elements, knowing the proper time and place, and understanding the stages of life and other factors,

then washed his feet and hands, performed the rites of purification, and— his desires fulfilled and his mind established in steadfastness— became cognizant of the proper time for the king’s meal. (25–26)
Having discerned the appropriate occasion for the king, one should cause food and other items to be served;
when they are wholesome for the king, one should introduce them gradually.
Herein, the various varieties of rice (*odana*) are first described by me.

The second is the variety of soups, and the third is that of clarified butter (sarpis). The fourth is the variety of side dishes, along with its elaborations. Here, the fifth is said to be meat and vegetables, together with their various subdivisions.
The sixth here is a variety of edible foods, and the seventh is that of milk-rice (pāyasa).
The eighth here is elixir (rasāyana), and the ninth is by way of varieties of drinks.
The tenth is a variety of soups (yūṣa), and [the eleventh] is a classification of food such as clarified butter (ghṛta) and so forth.
The eleventh is that of the linctus, and likewise the twelfth is the division of [medicinal] powders;
the thirteenth is the liquid, and the fourteenth is the division of milk;
the fifteenth is the division of curd, and the sixteenth is the division of buttermilk.
The sixteenth primary division has been demonstrated by way of illustration;
the intermediate subdivisions therein should be sought out by those of great intelligence according to their respective contexts.
Thus, the discussion has been set forth by me as appropriate for each particular case.
Indeed, in a place named Pānīya, there is the emergence of water;
furthermore, a wondrous thing is told, namely milk-rice (pāyasa) produced from sour [gruel].
Such various wonders and diverse tasks as these [are described]. ||34-35||
Those things that have been cooked should be made uncooked by the wise;
what is the use of much speaking on this matter? Listen, O Lord, to one appropriate point:
at whatever time and place, O King, there is indeed a disposition of compassion.
Thus, by means of that method, its origin has been explained. Food is said to be the primary life-force of all living beings;
it is truly the form of Brahman, consisting of sixty-three essences.
One should consume excellent food that is free from the eight defects;
for how can one attain freedom from those defects without first knowing their nature?
Since it is irreproachable and defectless, there is no defect residing therein. (39)
Therefore, there is indeed no eightfold defect here, according to the authority of the Śruti.
For the eightfold defect exists [only] through the error of perception;
what are those defects that are always present in powerful perception? (40–41)
Thus, for the sake of knowing the answer regarding the question posed according to the measurement of the eldest [brother]:
those defects which depend upon it— namely, being uncooked (*asṛta*), slimy (*picchila*), impure (*aśuci*),
boiled (*kvathita*), dried (*śuṣka*), burnt (*dagdha*), deformed (*virūpa*), and likewise not born of the proper season (*anartuja*).
And their defining characteristic (svarūpalakṣaṇa) is stated along with their qualities in due order.
What is the purpose of that investigation which takes the form of laughter?
Milk is abandoned by the virtuous because of its [status as] milk, while water is [discarded] by those expert in fluidity.
"This is defective, this is faultless, and this is [of] such-and-such [a nature]"—
it is for the sake of discerning this that a substance joined with a defect is [examined] with effort;
however, for one who has mastery over what is non-defective, this alone is the purpose.
There are no defects in food itself, nor do they ever arise from it;
rather, those defects certainly occur due to the negligence of the cook.
I shall now describe in order the characteristics and qualities of the eight types of defects.
If gruel has not been properly boiled, it is said that the food is uncooked;
if one eats such food, it will cause disease.
When food is overcooked, it becomes slimy and relies upon the digestive fire for its digestion.
The digestive fire of the stomach abandons that food by which one is nourished. Food that is joined with worms, hair, and other such things is considered impure;
from eating that, the tongue loses its relish and drips with water.
